5.subtopic: Ionic and Covalent Bonding, Lewis Structures and Octet Rule
5.solution: By Fajans' rules, a higher cation charge polarises the anion more and gives more covalent character. \(\mathrm{Pb^{4+}}\) in \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) carries the highest charge here, so \(\mathrm{PbCl_4}\) is the most covalent.

60.subtopic: Logical Equivalence and Algebra of Statements
60.solution:
\(p \to (q \to r) \equiv \sim p \vee \sim q \vee r\), which is also \((p \wedge q) \to r\) and \(q \to (p \to r)\): (I) and (IV) hold.

\((p \to q) \to r \equiv (p \wedge \sim q) \vee r\). But \(p \to (q \vee r) \equiv \sim p \vee q \vee r\) and \((p \to r) \wedge (\sim q \to r) \equiv (\sim p \wedge q) \vee r\), so (II) and (III) fail (try p T, q F, r F).

61.solution: The contrapositive of \(X \to Y\) is \(\sim Y \to \sim X\). \(\sim(p \wedge \sim q) \equiv \sim p \vee q\) and \(\sim[p \vee (p \to q)] \equiv \sim p \wedge \sim(p \to q) \equiv \sim p \wedge (p \wedge \sim q)\). That is option (D).

62.solution:
A converse is defined for a conditional, so first write \(p \vee q \equiv \sim p \to q\). Its converse is \(q \to \sim p \equiv \sim q \vee \sim p\), and the negation of that is \(p \wedge q\).

The question is ambiguous: if "converse" is taken to mean simply swapping the two parts, \(q \vee p\), its negation is \(\sim p \wedge \sim q\) (option D).
62.note: a converse is defined only for a conditional; reading p v q as ~p -> q gives B, while the key's D treats the converse as q v p, so the question has two defensible answers

On \([0, 1]\), \(uv\) ranges from 0 to \(\dfrac{\pi^2}{16}\), so \(u^3 + v^3\) ranges from \(\dfrac{\pi^3}{32}\) to \(\dfrac{\pi^3}{8}\). Hence \(\dfrac{1}{32} \le a \le \dfrac{1}{8}\); of the options, \(a \ge \dfrac{1}{32}\).
